This is quite weird.

The 'cs' string is the connection string returned by the C code inside
RODBC:

   stat <- .Call(C_RODBCDriverConnect, as.character(connection), id,
                 as.integer(believeNRows), as.logical(readOnlyOptimize))
   # ...
   cs <- attr(stat, "connection.string")
   if(grepl("PWD=", cs)) {
       # mask the password inside the returned object

RODBC passes the connection string back to R like this:

 #define buf1_len 8096
 // ...
 SQLCHAR buf1[buf1_len];
 // ...
 retval = SQLDriverConnect(
  thisHandle->hDbc, NULL,
  (SQLCHAR *)Rf_translateChar(STRING_ELT(connection, 0)),
  SQL_NTS,
  (SQLCHAR *)buf1, (SQLSMALLINT)buf1_len,
  &tmp1,
  SQL_DRIVER_NOPROMPT
 );
 if(retval == SQL_SUCCESS || retval == SQL_SUCCESS_WITH_INFO) {
  // ...
  PROTECT(constr = Rf_allocVector(STRSXP, 1));
  SET_STRING_ELT(constr, 0, Rf_mkChar((char *)buf1));
  // ...
  Rf_setAttrib(ans, Rf_install("connection.string"), constr);

Somehow, the 'buf1' string isn't filled at all and R receives
uninitialised stack contents instead of the effective connection
string, despite the return value indicates a successful connection. And
yet 'idbc' works using the same connection string, suggesting that the
problem isn't inside the MDBtools driver.

How did you install the RODBC package? If there's nothing obviously
wrong with your R package installation, further investigation will
probably require stepping through the C code in a debugger.

-- 
Best regards,
Ivan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

I think there are two separate things going on, and only one of them is RODBC's fault.

1. The warnings are probably harmless.

After connecting, odbcConnect() asks the driver to return the completed connection string and then runs grepl("PWD=", cs) on it so it can hide any password. The MDBTools ODBC driver doesn't seem to fill in that returned string properly, so R ends up reading whatever bytes happen to be in the buffer. That explains why the "unable to translate" garbage changes on every run. The connection itself is probably open. You can check with:

> connEOS <- odbcConnect("EOS")
> sqlQuery(connEOS, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM SomeRealTableName")

2. The empty sqlTables() result and the sqlFetch() failure are driver limitations.

MDBTools' implementation of the ODBC catalog functions (SQLTables and related calls) is minimal. sqlFetch() first calls odbcTableExists(), which relies on sqlTables(), so it fails even when the table exists. You can skip that check by querying directly:

> sqlQuery(connEOS, "SELECT * FROM SomeRealTableName") %>% as_tibble()

3. The bigger problem: vw_Prodotti is almost certainly an Access saved query, not a table.

MDBTools can only read tables. It cannot execute Access queries or views at all, so vw_Prodotti won't work through any route on Linux. If this worked two years ago, I'd guess you were running on Windows with the Microsoft Access driver, which does support queries. You can confirm this in isql: SELECT * FROM vw_Prodotti will fail there too, while selecting from the underlying tables will work.

The fix is to get the SQL behind the view and run it against the base tables yourself. mdbtools can show it from the shell (or from R via system()):

> system("mdb-queries -L EOS2024a.mdb")              # list saved queries
> system("mdb-queries EOS2024a.mdb vw_Prodotti")     # print its SQL
> system("mdb-tables -1 EOS2024a.mdb")               # list real tables

You may need to adjust the Access-flavored SQL slightly (for example IIf(), square brackets, or #date# literals) before MDBTools will accept it. Often it's simpler to pull the base tables into R and rebuild the joins in dplyr.

4. Alternatively, you can skip ODBC entirely.

For read-only extraction this is often more reliable:

> library(Hmisc)
> f <- "/datadisk/.../EOS2024a.mdb"
> mdb.get(f, tables = TRUE)                # list tables
> prod <- mdb.get(f, tables = "Prodotti")  # wraps mdb-export

Or call mdb-export yourself, e.g.:

> prod <- read_csv(pipe(paste("mdb-export", shQuote(f), "Prodotti")))

In short: the warnings are probably cosmetic, the table check fails because of MDBTools' weak catalog support, and the view fails because MDBTools can't run Access queries. Use sqlQuery() on the base tables and recreate the view from the SQL shown by mdb-queries.

HTH,
gregg

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Your three-machine test tells us a lot. You get the same failure on two Debian releases and on Kubuntu, with two different .mdb files (including your old small one). Meanwhile isql and the mdb-tools command line (via Hmisc::mdb.get) both read the data fine. That rules out the files, your RODBC install, and the unixODBC version. What’s left is how RODBC and the MDBTools ODBC driver work together. I think (possibly- but probably) two separate problems are being mistaken for one.

1. The garbage warning (cosmetic)

Ivan’s reading of the C code is right. As far as I can tell from the driver source, MDBTools’ SQLDriverConnect() connects using the Database= setting and returns SQL_SUCCESS, but it never writes the output connection string (szConnStrOut / pcbConnStrOut). RODBC doesn’t initialise buf1 before the call, so R receives whatever happened to be on the stack.

On your Debian boxes those leftover bytes probably start with a NUL or happen to be valid text, so grepl() stays quiet. On Kubuntu, with GCC 15 and a different stack layout, they aren’t. It’s the same bug on all three machines, but it’s only visible on one. It doesn’t affect the connection itself, and it isn’t why you get no data.

2. No rows returned (the real problem)

odbcConnect() defaults to believeNRows = TRUE and rows_at_time = 100. As far as I can tell, the MDBTools driver doesn’t return a usable row count for a SELECT, and it doesn’t support fetching many rows at once. With those defaults, RODBC can conclude there are zero rows and return an empty result. Give this a shot:

[R]
> library(RODBC)
> connEOS <- odbcConnect("EOS", believeNRows = FALSE, rows_at_time = 1)
> sqlTables(connEOS)
> sqlQuery(connEOS, "SELECT * FROM YourTableName", errors = TRUE)
> odbcGetErrMsg(connEOS)
> close(connEOS)

Use a real table name from mdb-tables yourfile.mdb in a shell. Depending on what you see:

- sqlQuery() returns data but sqlTables() is empty: that’s a separate gap in the driver’s table listing. Just name the tables directly.

- sqlQuery() works but sqlFetch() doesn’t: the likely cause is how RODBC quotes table names, which the MDBTools SQL parser handles poorly. Stick with sqlQuery().

[ODBC]
> Trace = Yes
> TraceFile = /tmp/odbc_trace.log

Rerun your R code, then look in /tmp/odbc_trace.log. You should see whether SQLDriverConnect leaves the output length unset and what SQLRowCount returns. Turn tracing off afterwards, because the log grows quickly. That log is also exactly what a maintainer would want attached to a bug report.

4. Where to report it

- RODBC: it has no public bug tracker. Running maintainer("RODBC") gives you the address. The fix is small: set buf1[0] = '\0' before the call, or check tmp1 before using buf1. Either way, RODBC shouldn’t trust a buffer the driver didn’t fill.

- MDBTools: report it at github.com/mdbtools/mdbtools/issues. Cover SQLDriverConnect not filling the output connection string and SQLRowCount on SELECT statements, and attach the trace.

5. If you’d rather avoid RODBC entirely

The odbc/DBI packages often cope better with drivers that have gaps like these:

[R]
> con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), dsn = "EOS")
> DBI::dbListTables(con)
> DBI::dbReadTable(con, "YourTableName")
> DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

Hmisc::mdb.get() also remains a perfectly good route, since it already works for you.

If believeNRows = FALSE with rows_at_time = 1 fixes it, I’d still send both reports. The warning is a real, if minor, bug in RODBC, and the next person to use MDBTools will hit the same empty results.

All the Best,
Gregg

messages.body_plain:
On 08/11/2026 17:46, Gregg Powell wrote:
> Hi Chris,
>
> Your three-machine test tells us a lot. You get the same failure on two Debian releases and on Kubuntu, with two different .mdb files (including your old small one). Meanwhile isql and the mdb-tools command line (via Hmisc::mdb.get) both read the data fine. That rules out the files, your RODBC install, and the unixODBC version. What’s left is how RODBC and the MDBTools ODBC driver work together. I think (possibly- but probably) two separate problems are being mistaken for one.
>
> 1. The garbage warning (cosmetic)
>
> Ivan’s reading of the C code is right. As far as I can tell from the driver source, MDBTools’ SQLDriverConnect() connects using the Database= setting and returns SQL_SUCCESS, but it never writes the output connection string (szConnStrOut / pcbConnStrOut). RODBC doesn’t initialise buf1 before the call, so R receives whatever happened to be on the stack.
>
> On your Debian boxes those leftover bytes probably start with a NUL or happen to be valid text, so grepl() stays quiet. On Kubuntu, with GCC 15 and a different stack layout, they aren’t. It’s the same bug on all three machines, but it’s only visible on one. It doesn’t affect the connection itself, and it isn’t why you get no data.
That's an even clearer explanation than the one from Ivan but I should 
have made it clearer that I realised that this has nothing to do with 
not pulling the data from the mdb.  I am interested that Kubuntu is 
doing things so differently but that's way above my IT savvy level!
>
> 2. No rows returned (the real problem)
>
> odbcConnect() defaults to believeNRows = TRUE and rows_at_time = 100. As far as I can tell, the MDBTools driver doesn’t return a usable row count for a SELECT, and it doesn’t support fetching many rows at once. With those defaults, RODBC can conclude there are zero rows and return an empty result. Give this a shot:
>
> [R]
>> library(RODBC)
>> connEOS <- odbcConnect("EOS", believeNRows = FALSE, rows_at_time = 1)
>> sqlTables(connEOS)
>> sqlQuery(connEOS, "SELECT * FROM YourTableName", errors = TRUE)
>> odbcGetErrMsg(connEOS)
>> close(connEOS)
> Use a real table name from mdb-tables yourfile.mdb in a shell. Depending on what you see:
>
> - sqlQuery() returns data but sqlTables() is empty: that’s a separate gap in the driver’s table listing. Just name the tables directly.
>
> - sqlQuery() works but sqlFetch() doesn’t: the likely cause is how RODBC quotes table names, which the MDBTools SQL parser handles poorly. Stick with sqlQuery().

That all worked perfectly with nothing in the error messages.

I didn't see the call you wanted for sqlFetch() but trying

sqlQuery(connEOS, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo_TabDistretto")

got

[1] CodDistretto             Descrizione              Valido                   CodArea                  CodSistemaEsterno        LastUser
[7] LastUp                   VisualizzaMotiviIngresso CodTipoScalaObbligatoria
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

Whereas

sqlQuery(connEOS, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo_TabDistretto")

got

sqlQuery(connEOS, "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM dbo_TabDistretto")

I am perfectly happy to stay with sqlQuery as it will clearly now do as 
well the DBI and Hmisc approaches with those " believeNRows = FALSE, 
rows_at_time = 1" arguments.

> [ODBC]
>> Trace = Yes
>> TraceFile = /tmp/odbc_trace.log
> Rerun your R code, then look in /tmp/odbc_trace.log. You should see whether SQLDriverConnect leaves the output length unset and what SQLRowCount returns. Turn tracing off afterwards, because the log grows quickly. That log is also exactly what a maintainer would want attached to a bug report.

I wasn't sure where you wanted those lines to go.  I guessed in 
/etc/odbcinst.ini and tried this

UsageCount=1

[MySQL ODBC 26.10 ANSI Driver]

UsageCount=1

Setup=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/odbc/libmdbodbc.so
FileUsage=1
UsageCount=1
Trace = Yes
TraceFile = /tmp/odbc_trace.log

[MDBToolsW]

Setup=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/odbc/libmdbodbcW.so

UsageCount=1
Trace = Yes
TraceFile = /tmp/odbc_trace.log

I also tried setting TraceFile to /home/chris/odbc_trace.log as R would 
have been running as user chris but neither version produced any trace.

> 4. Where to report it
>
> - RODBC: it has no public bug tracker. Running maintainer("RODBC") gives you the address. The fix is small: set buf1[0] = '\0' before the call, or check tmp1 before using buf1. Either way, RODBC shouldn’t trust a buffer the driver didn’t fill.
The maintainer, as I am sure you have seen is Professor Ripley and I 
have caught the sharp end of his tongue before and I honestly don't know 
what "set buf1[0] = '\0' before the call, or check tmp1 before using 
buf1" means so I would like, with your permission, to quote you.
> - MDBTools: report it at github.com/mdbtools/mdbtools/issues. Cover SQLDriverConnect not filling the output connection string and SQLRowCount on SELECT statements, and attach the trace.
But I have no trace!  If you can push me in the correct direction for 
that, I will do that.
>
> 5. If you’d rather avoid RODBC entirely
>
> The odbc/DBI packages often cope better with drivers that have gaps like these:
>
> [R]
>> con <- DBI::dbConnect(odbc::odbc(), dsn = "EOS")
>> DBI::dbListTables(con)
>> DBI::dbReadTable(con, "YourTableName")
>> DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
> Hmisc::mdb.get() also remains a perfectly good route, since it already works for you.
Yes, both of those work for me (thanks again) so this is about trying to 
be a good FLOSS user, not a nasty!
> If believeNRows = FALSE with rows_at_time = 1 fixes it, I’d still send both reports. The warning is a real, if minor, bug in RODBC, and the next person to use MDBTools will hit the same empty results.

Yes, the first is sort of a bug in the warning and the second is the 
more substantive bug in how RODBC cooperates with MDBTools?

Assuming so, yes I will, but see above.

>
> All the Best,

Many thanks again!

Hello again Chris,
Glad the main problem appears to be solved. Here's where I think things stand on the rest.

THE TRACE (my fault for being unclear)

The trace lines need their own section, headed by a line that just says [ODBC]. They don't go inside the driver sections. I suspect the [ODBC] header got lost in the formatting of my email. Please do this:

1. Remove the Trace and TraceFile lines you added under [MDBTools] and [MDBToolsW].

2. Add this block at the top of /etc/odbcinst.ini, header line included:

> [ODBC]
> Trace = Yes
> TraceFile = /tmp/odbc_trace.log

3. Check that /etc/odbcinst.ini is the file unixODBC is actually reading. Run this in a shell and look at the DRIVERS line:

> odbcinst -j

4. Restart R completely so the driver manager rereads its configuration. Then run your connect and query once more, using the defaults so the trace captures the failing case:

> library(RODBC)
> connEOS <- odbcConnect("EOS")
> sqlQuery(connEOS, "SELECT * FROM dbo_TabDistretto")
> close(connEOS)

5. This should now show a file:

> ls -l /tmp/odbc_trace.log

When you're done, set Trace = No.

In the log, look for the SQLDriverConnect exit. You should see the output connection string left empty or unset. Further down, look for SQLRowCount returning 0 even though the table has rows.

THE COUNT(*) RESULT

I'm not certain I'm reading your paste correctly, since the second command seems to have come through without its output. If the first result came from SELECT COUNT(*), though, it's telling us something: instead of a single count column, the driver returned the table's own column names with no rows. My guess is that MDBTools' SQL parser simply doesn't handle aggregates. It's a very limited SQL dialect, built for simple SELECT ... WHERE queries. If so, it isn't an RODBC problem. Do the counting in R instead:

> x <- sqlQuery(connEOS, "SELECT * FROM dbo_TabDistretto")
> nrow(x)

For the sqlFetch test I mentioned, this is the call:

> sqlFetch(connEOS, "dbo_TabDistretto")

WHICH BUG GOES WHERE

Your summary is nearly right, with one correction on the second item:

1. The garbage warning. I believe this is a small bug in RODBC: it trusts a buffer the driver never filled. MDBTools shares the blame, because it should fill that buffer and doesn't. It's worth reporting to both.

2. The empty results. This is really the driver's doing, not RODBC's. MDBTools reports a row count of 0 and can't fetch many rows at once. RODBC already has documented options for drivers like this (believeNRows and rows_at_time), so I wouldn't call it an RODBC bug. That one belongs on the MDBTools GitHub only. I'd leave it out of anything you send to Prof. Ripley.

QUOTING ME

Yes, quote me. In plain English, the fix means this: before RODBC asks the driver to fill in the connection-string buffer, it should put an empty string in it. Then, if the driver writes nothing, R gets "" instead of whatever random bytes were sitting in that memory. That's also the whole answer to why Kubuntu behaves differently. It isn't doing anything wrong. The random bytes left in memory just happen to differ there, and only on that machine are they bytes R can't turn into text.

If it helps, here's text you could send more or less as-is:

----- suggested text -----
With the MDBTools ODBC driver (odbc-mdbtools 1.0.x), odbcConnect() succeeds but produces warnings from grepl("PWD=", cs) about untranslatable strings. The driver's SQLDriverConnect() returns SQL_SUCCESS without writing to OutConnectionString or StringLength2Ptr, so in C_RODBCDriverConnect the uninitialised buf1 is passed to mkChar(). Initialising buf1[0] = '\0' (and tmp1 = 0) before the SQLDriverConnect() call, or only using buf1 when tmp1 > 0, would make RODBC robust to drivers that don't fill the output string. Seen with RODBC 1.3-26.3 on R 4.6.2 (Kubuntu 26.04) and R 4.5.3 / 4.2.2 (Debian 12). The warning is harmless; the connection works.
------------------------------

It's short, it identifies the exact cause, it proposes a fix, and it says up front that the problem is minor. From what I've seen- that's the kind of report maintainers handle without complaint.

For MDBTools, a GitHub issue covering three points, with the trace attached, would do it:

- SQLDriverConnect doesn't fill the output connection string.
- SQLRowCount returns 0 after a SELECT.
- Multi-row (block) fetches don't return rows; RODBC needs rows_at_time = 1.

If you keep running into an issue - just post the whole piece of code here if you'd like - that might be easier than going back and forth...
Best regard,
Gregg
